value: 256 Hz tuning fork held toward the web: escape in 58% of responses and attack in 36% (two years combined)
method: field behavioural assay on orb webs: a tuning fork (256 Hz or 440 Hz) struck on a plastic spray bottle and brought slowly towards the web to touch its frame, and an 8 cm wire touched to the back of the abdomen; behaviour scored as escape or attack; frequency distributions compared with Fisher's exact tests
conditions: Wild spiders in their webs at accessible sites in Southeast Wales, 8 Aug to 6 Sep 2020 and 1 to 17 Aug 2021; adult females, assumed to be M. segmentata, 4 to 9 mm long; 38 of 50 spiders analysed in 2020 and 40 of 46 in 2021 (spiders removed for insufficient data, mainly not returning between stimuli). No no-stimulus control: the wire was the comparison stimulus. Order was fixed in 2020 (256 Hz, 440 Hz, wire) and randomised in 2021 (random number generator); the paper reports the wire gave less consistent responses by order. 440 Hz forks provoked attacks in about 90% of responses (both years combined); highest no-response rate 16% (wire, 2020). Acoustic frequency is the stimulus label; the paper reports no measured vibration amplitude or sound level. In both years some spiders escaped from the 256 Hz fork before it touched the web (negative reaction times), which the authors attribute, untested, to air movement sensed by trichobothria, so the 256 Hz response is not purely to web vibration. Order did not affect responses to the forks (Fisher's exact p = 0.584 for 256 Hz, 0.333 for 440 Hz) but did for the wire (p = 0.033); responses did not differ between years (p = 0.81, 0.51, 0.49), which is the basis for combining them; spiders escaped faster than they attacked with the 256 Hz fork and attacked faster with the 440 Hz fork. A few individuals per site were confirmed as M. segmentata in the laboratory (M. mengei is hard to tell apart in the field).

source.title: The Use of Tuning Forks for Studying Behavioural Responses in Orb Web Spiders

quote: The 256 Hz tuning fork largely produces escape behaviours (58% of responses across the two years), although there was more variation with this tuning fork (36% showed attack behaviours).
note: Sentence returned in two abutting pieces in one response (said in pieces). Family printed in the paper (Tetragnathidae). Licence: page prints the Creative Commons Attribution (CC BY) license; Crossref CC BY 4.0, content-version vor. Page byline Mollie S. Davies and Thomas Hesselberg, as Crossref. The fork touches the web frame, so the stimulus is mainly web vibration, but the authors report pre-contact escapes to the 256 Hz fork and attribute them to air movement (Discussion); kept under sense_vibration with that caveat (audit 329). value: more active after exposure to waterborne chemical cues from its catfish prey; the prey (catfish) did not avoid chemical cues from the snakes
method: captive activity trials: 10 L of water from a tank holding nine striped eel catfish (Plotosus lineatus) or from an empty tank poured into one corner of the snakes' tank; activity scored as head crossings of cords in the 2 min after addition
conditions: Four wild-caught snakes (SVL 53 to 130 cm; sex not reported) from Baie des Citrons and Anse Vata, New Caledonia, January to March 2020, held 6 to 19 days in a seawater tank; stimulus order (catfish water versus control) randomised, trials 15 to 30 min apart, daytime. Snakes were about twice as active with catfish water (F1,4 = 53.57, p < 0.006, linear mixed model). Conditioning time of the catfish water and fasting state of the snakes are not stated. Catfish shelter-choice trials (nine fish, 15 replicates, 7 control versus 8 snake-scented choices, chi-square 0.06, p = 0.79) showed no avoidance; all nine catfish stayed together in every trial, so the 15 replicates are choices by one swarm, and the authors note pseudoreplication (same fish and same scented cloth in successive trials). Only catfish-scented and empty-tank water were tested ('For logistical reasons'), with no water from a non-prey fish, so the result shows a response to catfish-conditioned water, not prey specificity. Tongue-flicking rates were scored 'where possible' and the Results say only that the increased activity was accompanied by high rates of tongue extrusion, with no counts or test. Each trial began after the snake had been inactive for at least 1 min; snake ID was a random effect. The snake response is activity, not a measured detection threshold or an identified receptor route.

value: trans-2-hexen-1-ol elicited the strongest antennal (EAG) response among the sweet-corn volatiles tested
method: electroantennogram of female antennae to four maize volatiles (hexanal, trans-2-hexen-1-ol, linalool, beta-caryophyllene) at 0.1, 1, 10 and 100 mg/mL in mineral oil; mineral oil blank and 100 mg/mL cis-3-hexen-1-ol positive control; 10 uL on filter paper; fixed sequence per antenna CK, CF, the four doses in ascending order, then CF, CK; relative response = (treatment - CK)/(CF - CK) x 100; one-way ANOVA with Tukey's test
conditions: Insects from eggs supplied by the National Plant Protection Scientific Observation and Experiment Station, Langfang, reared on artificial diet; n = 5 female antennae per substance, 45 s between stimuli; doses were given in fixed ascending order, never randomised (Methods 2.6), so concentration is confounded with presentation order; female age is not stated. Results 3.4 says mated and unmated females were tested: mated females gave significantly higher EAG responses than unmated females at 100 mg/mL hexanal and beta-caryophyllene and at 10 mg/mL trans-2-hexen-1-ol, with no significant difference at the other concentrations (Table 2S); n per mating group is not given. The abstract says FAW adults while the Methods describe female antennae only. Amplitudes are reported as relative EAG responses (%) in Fig 4 and Table S2, which were not read, so no statistics were seen for the ranking; the Results text says responses of females to the four substances increased with concentration.

value: adult males were attracted to volatiles of honeydew excreted by adult males (74% response rate); females were not
method: Y-plate two-choice olfactometer: honeydew on filter paper (5 mm x 10 mm) in one arm against clean hexane-cleaned filter paper in the other; non-choosers within 3 min counted as non-responders; G-test
conditions: Adults captured weekly from the field (Ailanthus altissima, Lehigh County, Pennsylvania) and shipped overnight, 19 August to 27 September 2019 (Early, Mid and Late phases for the collections overall), but the honeydew bioassays used four of those weeks, three Early (after adult emergence) and one Mid (mating), and no Late-phase insects; fed cut A. altissima branches, no starvation described. Honeydew was collected in the field from groups of 20 males or 20 females sleeved on A. altissima for 48 h; each week one session tested 10 males and 10 females (alternating) to male honeydew and another the same to female honeydew. Males tested with male honeydew: G = 13.72, df = 1, alpha = 0.001, n = 35, overall response rate 74%; the paper gives no n or G for females, only that they were not attracted. Sexes were tested in alternating order, five control insects without stimulus per session checked olfactometer bias, and the stimulus and control arms were reversed in the next session on a clean Y-plate (randomisation is not described); dedicated no-stimulus control sessions showed low response rates and no directional bias. Honeydew from females did not significantly attract either sex, though both sexes showed a trend towards attraction that approached significance. Synthetic compounds were tested separately and are not logged here.

value: males were significantly attracted to female-conditioned water in the mating period (chi-square 4.12, P = 0.04) but not in the non-mating period (chi-square 0.31, P = 0.58)
method: Y-maze with crude female-conditioned water in one arm against ultrapure water in the other; one test per animal, 5 min window; chi-square test
conditions: Males bought in Guilin, Guangxi, China in August 2020 (farmed or wild origin not stated) (mean weight 16.22 +/- 1.82 g) and held without contact with females or pheromones; non-mating-period (NMP) males fed until January 2021 at water temperature below 15 C and mating-period (MP; 'the initial stage of the MP') males until April 2021 at above 22 C, so the two groups were tested months apart at different temperatures; 50 males per period. Conditioned water: 20 mature females (bought with the males in August 2020; mating state not stated) were fasted 48 h, then held 24 h in 1 L ultrapure water at 23 to 25 C; the water was centrifuged 20 min (8000 rpm, 4 C) and stored at -80 C until the assays, so the stimulus was frozen for months before the January and April tests and its collection date is not given; 1 ml on a sponge in one arm against 1 ml ultrapure water, in 500 ml of water flowing at 20 ml/min. Arm positions swapped after every five animals; animals making no choice in 5 min were counted as unresponsive and excluded, and their number is not reported, nor are the arm counts in the text. The conditioned water is a crude mixture, not a single compound.
